questions.q: What does a table's prefix (like AP_, AR_, GL_) tell you?
options: Nothing useful
Which product/module owns the table
The table's row count
The physical database server
questions.explain: Oracle Fusion table prefixes consistently identify the owning module, e.g. AP_ for Payables and GL_ for General Ledger.

questions.q: What does the _ALL suffix on a table name mean?
options: The table includes rows for every business unit/operating context at once
The table has no primary key
The table is deprecated
The table only stores a single row
questions.explain: The _ALL suffix is a multi-org holdover meaning the table spans every business unit, so queries must scope it deliberately to avoid mixing unrelated data.

questions.q: What is the standard shape of a primary key column name?
options: It always starts with PK_
It almost always ends in _ID, e.g. INVOICE_ID or PARTY_ID
It is always a single letter
It always matches the table name exactly
questions.explain: Primary keys consistently end in _ID, and foreign keys typically repeat that same column name on the child table.

It is used internally for optimistic locking, not business reporting
It is the table's primary key
It records the invoice amount
questions.explain: OBJECT_VERSION_NUMBER helps prevent two users from silently overwriting each other's changes — it's an internal locking mechanism, not a reporting column.

questions.q: What is true about flexfield columns like ATTRIBUTE1 or SEGMENT1?
options: Their meaning is fixed and identical across every Oracle Fusion customer
They are never used in financial tables
They are generic, configurable slots whose actual meaning is set per implementation
They always store the creation date
questions.explain: Flexfield segment/attribute columns are configurable per implementation (e.g., a chart-of-accounts segment for cost center), so the column name alone never tells you what it means.
